title: The Six-Minute Dilemma: Litera's Avaneesh Marwaha on Building Legal Tech That Actually Gets Used The Geek in Review
author: Avaneesh Marwaha · Marcie Borgal Shunk

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Marwaha does not substantively accept the cluster’s apprenticeship-risk framing. Although he recognises verification costs and calls for training and adaptation, he primarily reframes automation as a selective means to remove unwanted routine work, expand capacity and enable more proactive legal advice rather than as a threat requiring reconstructed apprenticeship.
qs: If they got to check the work over and over again, you start losing some of that value over time.
You’ll pivot, you’ll train, you’ll educate, and you’ll keep moving forward.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Marwaha does not address the cluster’s central model of organisational redesign around repeatable, scalable legal services. He instead frames GenAI chiefly as augmentation that frees existing lawyers from routine work so they can meet latent demand and provide earlier, more proactive advice, without reducing professional headcount.
qs: I think GenAI can help augment a lot of the stuff that doesn’t need to happen.
Get lawyers in the room when decisions are being made so we can de-risk bad ideas.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source distinguishes individual productivity gains from consistent organizational adoption, aligning with the cluster’s staging of experimentation and deployment. However, it does not address access to justice, service transformation, or whether adoption can close justice gaps, so its position on the central proposition cannot be determined.
qs: And that’s allowed me to go a lot faster.

So I’m curious from your perspective, what is a tactic or at least one tactic that is  Marlene Gebauer (15:00)  You  Marcie Borgal Shunk (15:12)  helping law firms move from this curiosity to a consistent use model.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source frames the AI boom as an opportunity to reposition Litera’s established products and pursue long-planned capabilities. It does not provide enough evidence on multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification, task-specific evaluation or reliable service outcomes to establish a position on the cluster’s central proposition.
qs: I think we felt looking in as a chairman saying this is exciting because all the hype being created with the new startups and with OpenAI, ChatGPT and Harvey, it created an opportunity for us to reposition our products, actually build what we wanted to build for a long time and felt like customers were ready for it.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Marwaha accepts the cluster’s bounded, human-led model and materially develops it by identifying fit-for-purpose workflows, arguing that verification can eliminate gains in complex drafting, and linking preservation of apprenticeship to the premium value clients expect from firms. He anticipates automation freeing lawyers for higher-value proactive work rather than autonomous delivery or broad lawyer replacement.
qs: I think it’s probably like 20 % of things could be automated or should be automated, and you can do it with high degree of trust today.

But as soon as I know that they’ve got rid of their hiring practices and gone to GenAI as soon as I know that their apprenticeship is dead, all that stuff’s gone, what’s the value of that shoe white glove service?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Marwaha accepts the cluster’s core augmentation and selective-deployment proposition, distinguishing valuable routine uses from unreliable long-form legal drafting and emphasising continued verification. He materially extends it with the “six-minute dilemma”: deployment must produce immediate, granular ROI and interoperate cleanly with existing systems or lawyers will revert to familiar workflows.
qs: And that’s the only way I think you make good product right now is thinking really minutia of the impact you’re making and the ROI you get from that.
You can use it for maybe checking and other things, but you can’t use it for the creation of 200 page M&A document with 100 % confidence.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Marwaha supports the cluster’s cautious account of agentic delegation: bounded workflow segments may be managed by agents, but repeated human verification can erase drafting gains. His emphasis on integrated tools and selective adoption also aligns with the cluster’s view that orchestration matters more than autonomy claims alone, while his product discussion provides plans rather than measured evidence of broad reliability.
qs: If they got to check the work over and over again, you start losing some of that value over time.
There are areas inside the workflow that can be  100 % managed with agents and skills and then other areas where we can use to do some deep research, some Q&A, all make sense.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Marwaha supports the cluster’s workflow-specific, human-checkpoint framing: he favours selective automation in targeted matter and business-development workflows rather than indiscriminate GenAI deployment, and stresses that repeated verification can erase value for experienced lawyers. His claims are managerial judgments without measured validation and do not resolve the broader difficulty of transferring tacit expertise.
qs: I think it’s probably like 20 % of things could be automated or should be automated, and you can do it with high degree of trust today.
If they got to check the work over and over again, you start losing some of that value over time.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between rapid product expansion and demonstrated value. Wilkins’s inventory growth partly reflects improved discovery of existing companies and features, while the agentic count tracks announcements rather than verified capabilities. Marwaha describes AI publicity as a commercial opening for Litera, but provides no adoption, effectiveness or renewal evidence.
qs: And so we published that in the beginning of March and we got such an overwhelming response, either from companies we didn’t know about or companies who had Gen.AI features that we didn’t know about, that we decided to rush and do another update to the map just two weeks later to coincide with Legal Week.

I think we felt looking in as a chairman saying this is exciting because all the hype being created with the new startups and with OpenAI, ChatGPT and Harvey, it created an opportunity for us to reposition our products, actually build what we wanted to build for a long time and felt like customers were ready for it.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Marwaha supports outcome-focused, fit-for-purpose AI adoption that releases capacity for proactive and unmet client work rather than merely automating existing tasks or reducing headcount. His account also reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on adjusted pricing, partnership incentives as an implementation barrier, and the still-prospective nature of broader transformation.
qs: I think there’s clients out there, including Litera, that have work firms could do for us, and we don’t even do them, to be compliant.
It’s gonna make the industry much more proactive and not reactive.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Marwaha aligns with the cluster’s framing of AI as an operating-model and expertise-development challenge rather than straightforward lawyer substitution. He expects routine associate work to be automated and advocates training and adaptation, but does not directly analyse succession risks or provide evidence that new training routes will preserve partner development.
qs: But it’s not because I want to reduce the size of lawyers and partners.
You’ll pivot, you’ll train, you’ll educate, and you’ll keep moving forward.

st.t: Legal consolidation: Acquisitions create integration work first
st.an: Marwaha’s emphasis on substantial internal development and selective acquisitions aligns with the cluster’s view that build and buy are complementary strategic choices rather than a simple binary. He supports acquiring only capabilities that materially advance Litera’s roadmap, although this excerpt does not directly address post-acquisition integration work or implementation-service boundaries.
qs: In the comments that I’m buy versus build, we are building a ton.
We’ve got to buy something that has to be innovative and really lead frogs our existing road map in some way.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Marwaha directly supports the cluster’s view that AI can augment legal work by taking on busy work and allowing lawyers to focus on harder problems. His three-to-five-year horizon is explicitly aspirational, consistent with the cluster’s conclusion that employment and task-allocation outcomes remain forecasts rather than measured effects.
qs: And three to five years, hopefully we’ll do more of that work and less of the work we do today.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Marwaha supports the cluster’s core claim that AI value depends on selective, workflow-specific implementation rather than indiscriminate model access. He reinforces its emphasis on trusted use cases and verification costs, while identifying business development and matter workflows as practical near-term priorities.
qs: If they got to check the work over and over again, you start losing some of that value over time.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Marwaha directly supports the cluster’s account of legal-AI adoption as organisational change shaped by incentives, entrenched practices and professional insecurity rather than tool quality alone. He also aligns with its prescriptions to focus on practical value and manage role transitions through training, although his claims rely mainly on anecdote and forecasts rather than measured transformation outcomes.
qs: But when you’re in a partnership model,  where generational partners own the wallet and want to protect their bonuses or don’t want to move their cheese because that’s how they did it and they feel like if you don’t do it their way you’re not a good lawyer.
You’ll pivot, you’ll train, you’ll educate, and you’ll keep moving forward.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Marwaha supports the cluster’s task-sensitive account: GenAI may assist with bounded or commoditized work, but complex drafting still requires costly human verification. He also reinforces the proposition that AI-driven staffing changes could undermine apprenticeship and the premium-service business model, rather than simply replacing lawyers wholesale.
qs: You can use it for maybe checking and other things, but you can’t use it for the creation of 200 page M&A document with 100 % confidence.

But as soon as I know that they’ve got rid of their hiring practices and gone to GenAI as soon as I know that their apprenticeship is dead, all that stuff’s gone, what’s the value of that shoe white glove service?

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s account of a rapidly expanding legal-AI map while clarifying that growth partly reflects improved directory coverage, not necessarily new launches, adoption or revenue. Her tracking of announced agentic offerings also supports treating market labels and counts cautiously, although she does not materially address disciplined procurement or implementation.
qs: And so we published that in the beginning of March and we got such an overwhelming response, either from companies we didn’t know about or companies who had Gen.AI features that we didn’t know about, that we decided to rush and do another update to the map just two weeks later to coincide with Legal Week.

But we also gave a sneak peek with this map into something else we’re working on, which will come up very shortly, which is a similar logo map that will encompass all of the products that have announced agentic AI offerings.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: Marwaha supports the cluster’s account that generative AI is changing vendors’ internal development economics and making build-versus-buy decisions more selective, while not eliminating acquisitions. His evidence is company experience and does not independently address or establish the cluster’s integration, migration and adoption constraints.
qs: So earlier this year, we brought a lot of AI tooling into our R&D organization to support, to change how we run a business.
We’re just much more mindful of, is this a long standing innovative product feature or is it a data play, is it a platform?

kp.k: Directory counts show expanding generative AI product offerings
kp.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports Legal Technology Hub’s directory mapping: 400 Gen.AI-powered products across 17 categories as of February 19th, published March 6th; 505 products across 18 categories in an update two weeks later; and 638 product placements from over 500 vendors across 19 categories as of June 26th. The early increase included previously unknown companies and features, rather than solely new launches. The latest map added AI governance; a separate map in preparation counted over a hundred announced agentic offerings, not verified deployments.
qs: We had 400 Gen.AI-powered products in the directory across 17 different categories.
in those two weeks, that initial 400 products grew to 505 products across 18 different categories.
And as of June 26th, it features 638 Gen. AI product placements by over 500 different vendors across 19 different categories.
But so far, we’re over a hundred of them.

kp.k: AI changes vendor development and acquisition economics
kp.d: Marwaha says competition from new AI software companies prompted Litera, with 1,200 employees and 500 in R&D, to introduce AI tooling into development earlier that year. He describes increased internal building and leadership changes, while retaining acquisitions for innovative products, data or platforms that materially advance its roadmap rather than readily reproducible features. These are the vendor CEO’s strategic assessments.
qs: And we have 1,200 people, at Litera. 500 R&D.
So earlier this year, we brought a lot of AI tooling into our R&D organization to support, to change how we run a business.
We just can’t buy features for the sake of features anymore.
We can make those pretty quickly.

kp.k: Internal adoption emphasizes outcomes and employee champions
kp.d: Asked about daily AI use, Marwaha describes measuring meaningful adoption through work quality, faster decisions and questioning unnecessary delays, rather than nominal usage. Employees share use cases and propose departmental tools through a working group, with development checking safety and security before rollout. He reports greater output than in January without employee growth, but supplies no quantified productivity measure.
qs: I think we, we realize the value when we see the quality of work increase or we see decision making get faster
And then we validate that with development and make sure it’s safe and secure.
So it’s not just top down. It’s a bottoms up approach of finding champions that really want to drive change long-term.
So I can tell you the output that we have at Litera today is much greater than it was in January.
and our business has not grown in employee size.

kp.k: Vendor agents reportedly accelerate coding and customer support
kp.d: Marwaha reports value from autonomous developers and support agents that triage tickets faster than humans, framing them as augmentation rather than elimination of skills. He illustrates potential customer-response improvement from three days to approximately an hour. His personal uses include meeting transcripts, research and financial scenario analysis within a secure internal Copilot, allowing him to undertake work previously delegated to others. These are operational anecdotes, not controlled evaluations.
qs: As a business, we’re finding huge value in autonomous developers that can go build code on their own.
We’re finding huge value opportunity and support where autonomous agents can handle support tickets and triage problems much more quickly than humans can.
May have waited three days for a wholesome response, or now getting at least a wholesome response in maybe an hour.
So a lot of my time has gone into maybe not asking for help, asking somebody to do something for me, I just do it myself.

kp.k: Pilot fatigue may temporarily depress legal AI adoption
kp.d: Marwaha asserts that $3 billion in venture capital focused on GenAI has entered the legal ecosystem. Although he welcomes innovation, he says repeated testing and piloting now burden firms and lawyers. Drawing on customer conversations over the preceding three months, he predicts a plateau or decline in adoption for new use cases; this is a forecast grounded in reported conversations, not a measured market trend.
qs: $3 billion of venture capital money has entered our ecosystem, focused on GenAI
most teams are getting tired of testing, testing, piloting, testing.
We’re going to go through a period now, I believe, of plateau or even depression of using generative AI for new use cases because of the fatigue that is set in
That’s happening and talking to customers in the last three months, fatigue is setting in.

kp.k: Native workflows and immediate reliability determine practical adoption
kp.d: Marwaha recommends embedding AI in Word and Outlook rather than requiring lawyers to switch applications. His 'six minute dilemma' describes lawyers’ short tolerance for friction: a failed or slow tool can lose out to familiar manual work, even if its potential output is valuable. He presents immediate task-level impact and return on investment as product-design criteria, not as a measured six-minute adoption threshold.
qs: Tooling, the model, the machine, all of those things have to be inside the native workflows that people are using today.
I don’t want to ask people to go anywhere else to do their job.
If you have attorneys and partners, they work in six minute mindset, right? Everything has to in six minutes. If it breaks in one, we’re done, we walk away.
Are we making an impact within six minutes? Is it taking longer than six minutes?

kp.k: Interoperability supports useful agents and customer value
kp.d: Responding to the Lexis–Harvey alliance, Marwaha treats ecosystem integration as an expected vendor responsibility that makes data more useful and may improve adoption. He advocates open APIs. He also argues that agents operate more cleanly in an integrated ecosystem: Litera’s experience data, document parsing and pricing tools support customer-co-built prototypes for actions following incoming emails, with releases expected in August or the next roughly 60 days. These are planned capabilities, not established customer outcomes.
qs: if data flows more easily, it’s more meaningful and actually has value and potentially better adoption of the tools.
So we believe that every API should be open to everybody.
And they’re all being co-built with customers.
if vendors don’t build robust APIs to allow the agents or skills to be used by anybody, you’re gonna have a not clean experience.

kp.k: Business development offers nearer-term gains than universal automation
kp.d: Marwaha rejects putting GenAI into every feature. Referring to Litera’s feature set, he estimates that around 20% could or should be automated with high trust today. He prioritizes partners’ business development, client identification and basic matter workflows, with some areas fully agent-managed and others supported by research or Q&A. He argues that experienced lawyers may already draft faster and more reliably themselves once verification burdens are considered.
qs: Not everything requires generative AI.
I think it’s probably like 20 % of things could be automated or should be automated, and you can do it with high degree of trust today.
If they got to check the work over and over again, you start losing some of that value over time.
Where I do want to apply the application, where we’re focused on it, is on business development activities, it’s basic workflow management of your matters.

kp.k: Existing document automation limits incremental generative AI value
kp.d: Marwaha notes that high-volume, low-impact documents already use question-and-answer automation supplied by vendors for decades, including estate documents. He says such work is already commoditized and often flat-fee, questioning the incremental return from adding GenAI. He nevertheless regards commoditized work as its safest application because of abundant data; his assertion of minimal error is not accompanied by testing evidence.
qs: You answer a set 10 questions, then you can do a binder of documents. That already exists today, right?
What’s the ROI from something that’s already heavily automated?
It’s already commoditized, it’s already become a flat fee.
But to me, that’s where GenAI is the safest place to live, where it’s commoditized because the error rate, we de minimis because the volume of data is so great.

kp.k: Complex drafting retains verification costs across associate levels
kp.d: Marwaha argues that GenAI is not yet fit for confidently creating 200-page M&A documents, describing incomplete generation and hallucination in documents of 200–300 pages. He contends that first-, third- and fifth-year associates and partners still need to review the work, negating the gains he sees from generation today. He allows checking uses and speculates that confidence might exceed 95% in two or three years; neither current errors nor future confidence are presented as benchmark results.
qs: you can’t use it for the creation of 200 page M&A document with 100 % confidence.
Because now a first year associate still has to proofread it. A third year associate still has to proofread it.
a fifth year associate will still proofread it and then a partner will get it.
Maybe in two or three years we’ll get to a point where it’s 95 % plus confidence, but not today.

kp.k: Premium clients may resist replacing apprenticeship with AI
kp.d: Speaking as a buyer, Marwaha estimates Litera spends $5–$15 million annually on legal fees through one primary and two secondary firms. He links the primary firm’s premium to bespoke treatment, expertise, dependable problem ownership and continued hiring and apprenticeship. He says substitution with GenAI that undermines that experience would lead him to seek a cheaper firm. This is one client’s stated purchasing preference, not evidence of general client behavior.
qs: Litera spends, I think, from $5 to $15 million a year on legal fees.
My primary firm wants me to believe I get everything bespoke.
As soon as that feeling goes away, I have a new primary firm that’s cheaper.

But as soon as I know that they’ve got rid of their hiring practices and gone to GenAI as soon as I know that their apprenticeship is dead, all that stuff’s gone, what’s the value of that shoe white glove service?

kp.k: Partnership incentives and job insecurity impede technological change
kp.d: Marwaha attributes slow adoption partly to established equity partners protecting bonuses and customary practices, and partly to back-office staff fearing displacement of infrastructure and training responsibilities. He illustrates the latter with a recent customer’s concern about desktop-image testing during cloud migration. He advocates a growth mindset, retraining and organizational renewal through new partners and firms; these are his causal interpretation and recommendations.
qs: where generational partners own the wallet and want to protect their bonuses or don’t want to move their cheese
What happens to all the roles that have been built for the last 30 years supporting an infrastructure that’s now changing?
but there are some that are still back office led.
You’ll pivot, you’ll train, you’ll educate, and you’ll keep moving forward.

kp.k: Automation could expand proactive legal work rather than headcount cuts
kp.d: Looking three to five years ahead, Marwaha hopes background workflows triggered by client actions will free lawyers for thinking, learning, relationship-building and early risk prevention. He argues that clients including Litera have additional compliance and environmental work firms could perform if capacity and appropriately adjusted fees were available. His forecast favors augmentation and expanded enterprise demand rather than fewer lawyers or partners, and is explicitly aspirational.
qs: I think we’ll get to a spot, hopefully in three years, maybe five, where work happens.
And that thing that’s happening isn’t the actual work, but it’s giving the partner and the attorneys thinking time.

And we had more active firms calling us and had their fees adjusted because the work they’re doing for us is different than M&A. I could keep firms busy for a long time, but they can’t even get to that work today.
But it’s not because I want to reduce the size of lawyers and partners. It’s because I think there’s so much for them to do.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source describes expanding legal-AI supply, productivity gains within a legal-tech vendor, selective automation of law-firm workflows, and a longer-term shift toward proactive legal services rather than wholesale lawyer replacement.
pts.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports growth in Legal Technology Hub's directory from 400 GenAI products across 17 categories as of February 19 to 505 across 18 categories in the subsequent map update, and 638 product placements from over 500 vendors across 19 categories as of June 26. She also reports over 100 products with announced agentic offerings. These are directory counts and announcements, not measures of adoption or performance. Avaneesh Marwaha says AI has increased Litera's output without increasing employee numbers, accelerated support and development, and enabled him to undertake research and financial analysis himself. He says faster internal feature development changes the rationale for acquisitions: Litera will still buy, but seeks innovative products, data or platforms rather than readily built features. For law firms, he predicts a near-term plateau or decline in new GenAI use cases because of pilot fatigue. He argues that adoption requires embedding tools in existing workflows, particularly Word and Outlook, and integrating data across the ecosystem. His estimate that roughly 20% could or should be automated with high trust refers to Litera's feature and function offering, not all legal work. He prioritises business development, matter workflow management, research and Q&A, with some workflow areas fully managed by agents. He questions GenAI's incremental value in already automated, commoditised documentation and its current value for creating long, complex M&A documents when repeated human verification remains necessary. Looking ahead, he predicts that background automation will free lawyers to think, advise and address currently uncommissioned corporate work, making the industry more proactive rather than eliminating it.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of directory curation, Marwaha's operational experience and customer conversations, product-development examples, and his experience buying legal services; the transcript supplies no controlled performance studies.
pts.d: Wilkins attributes the map's expansion partly to learning about previously unknown companies and GenAI features following the first release, so the count increases do not solely establish newly created products. Marwaha reports greater Litera output than in January at unchanged headcount, but gives no output metric or comparison design. His support example contrasts a possible three-day wait with a response in perhaps an hour; it is an operational illustration, not a reported aggregate benchmark. His fatigue prediction draws on conversations with customers over the preceding three months. His agentic-workflow claims draw on customer co-development, prototypes and forthcoming products linking Litera's matter-experience data, document parsing and pricing capabilities; he does not provide measured law-firm implementation results. His reservations about complex drafting rely on his account of hallucinations and successive associate and partner checks, rather than a quantified hallucination study. His assertion that commoditised tasks have minimal errors because of abundant data is likewise an opinion without reported testing. His view that premium firms risk losing value if they abandon bespoke service and apprenticeship draws on Litera's reported annual legal expenditure of $5–15 million and his own purchasing preferences. His expectation of additional demand draws on work he says Litera could commission if firms had capacity and appropriate fees. The claim that $3 billion of venture capital has entered the GenAI legal ecosystem is not accompanied by a source or measurement period.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Marwaha distinguishes current selective benefits from forthcoming product releases, tentative improvements in complex drafting in two to three years, and an aspirational three-to-five-year transformation of legal workflows.
pts.d: The discussion is framed in 2025. Wilkins's directory snapshot is dated June 26, with a further quarterly update planned for late September. Marwaha's internal productivity comparison runs from January to the interview. His forecast of adoption fatigue concerns the immediate period ahead and follows customer conversations during the prior three months. He presents native-workflow integration, reliable APIs, rapid visible value and limited verification burden as conditions for sustained use: a tool that fails or takes too long within lawyers' six-minute working mindset may be abandoned for the old method. His recommended near-term opportunities are business development and routine workflow management, not universal GenAI deployment. Litera's agentic products are described as forthcoming in August or approximately the next 60 days, rather than as established deployments with measured results. He regards complex-document creation as not fit for purpose today and speculates that it may reach '95 % plus confidence' in two or three years; he does not define that confidence as a benchmark metric. He expects adoption to remain slow while established partners control investment and resist changing practices, and also identifies back-office job insecurity as a barrier. His more automatic, less product-visible workflow future is explicitly hopeful and placed three to five years out. Capturing additional corporate demand depends on firms having time, approaching clients proactively and adjusting fees to the work involved.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern legal-tech vendors and their employees, law-firm partners and associates, technology-support teams, and corporate clients; the predicted gains chiefly involve capacity, service experience and additional business-law work.
pts.d: For Litera and other vendors, AI changes development capacity, acquisition choices, integration requirements and competition from new entrants. Litera's developers and support personnel are described as augmented, while customers receive faster responses. Within firms, partners and rainmakers are proposed beneficiaries of business-development automation; associates and partners could avoid routine administrative steps and gain thinking time. However, Marwaha says complex drafting still requires successive human checks, limiting current savings, and argues that experienced lawyers may already draft faster and with greater trust themselves. Premium firms face a purchasing risk in his personal account: removing apprenticeship and replacing bespoke service with GenAI could make him switch to a cheaper provider. Established equity partners and back-office personnel can impede adoption because of financial incentives, established practices or concerns about their roles. His example of desktop-image testing and training concerns cloud and infrastructure change as well as AI, not demonstrated AI job displacement. Corporate clients such as Litera could obtain more proactive compliance, risk-management and environmental-related assistance if firms free capacity and price it appropriately. This is latent enterprise demand, not an access-to-justice claim about underserved individuals. His preferred future preserves lawyers and partners while redirecting their work rather than reducing their numbers.
